morningSummary:
Tuesday, 17 November 2026 — Midday News & Global Update. Updated at 12:29 Europe/Paris. The midday edition reflects developments confirmed since the morning briefing, with a focus on the Quad leaders' meeting in Manila, the planned Trump-Xi-Putin meeting in Shenzhen, new US-China technology tensions, Ukraine's overnight attacks, France's public-sector strike and the 2027 presidential debate, the UK's changing Brexit discussion, Canada's trade engagement with China, and important opposition and accountability questions in Nigeria.

ASIA-PACIFIC AND GLOBAL DIPLOMACY — Donald Trump has met the leaders of Japan, India and Australia in Manila for the first Quad leaders' meeting since his return to the White House. Public remarks identify maritime security, critical minerals, energy resilience and AI as priorities. China has warned it will take necessary measures after Washington tightened controls on remote access to advanced AI chips through overseas data centres. The technology dispute is unfolding as Xi Jinping prepares to host Trump and Vladimir Putin for a planned trilateral meeting in Shenzhen on 19 November. The meeting has not yet taken place and no agreement has been announced. China and Canada have also expanded targeted tariff concessions after Carney's meeting with Xi. France and Malaysia announced a strategic partnership including rare-earth cooperation. Papua New Guinea's prime minister voiced support for China's reunification position on Taiwan; that statement does not settle Taiwan's status.

EUROPE, UKRAINE AND FRANCE — Ukrainian officials report damage to Kyiv's underground railway and critical infrastructure after overnight attacks. Russia says it targeted military-industrial sites and energy infrastructure; the Russian account is attributed and should not be treated as independent verification of every target. In France, public-sector unions are striking over pay and purchasing power, with transport and port disruption reported in several regions. Marine Le Pen is presenting pension proposals, but the National Rally's promised savings remain campaign claims subject to scrutiny by investors and economists. In the UK, Prime Minister Andy Burnham says Brexit weakened Britain's global standing and wants a long-term discussion with the EU after the 20 November summit. No immediate return to the EU has been announced. EU foreign ministers are also backing work towards an upgraded association framework with Syria, which remains a fragile transition.

MIDDLE EAST — Germany and the EU are pressing Israel to allow substantially more humanitarian aid into Gaza before winter. The EU says flooding and winter conditions are worsening living conditions and calls for sustained access, civilian protection and the reopening of crossings. Separately, UKMTO recorded an unidentified projectile striking a merchant vessel near the Strait of Hormuz and causing an engine-room fire. All crew were accounted for; no attacker or weapon has been identified. Oman and Iran have discussed maritime safety, but no agreement restoring normal commercial passage has been announced.

NIGERIA — The ADC leadership dispute remains unresolved. Nafiu Bala Gombe has offered conditional reconciliation to Atiku Abubakar and David Mark, while the Mark-led faction's appeal and stay application remain separate legal steps. Premium Times reported that no court order granting a stay had been obtained as of Monday; an appeal alone does not automatically suspend a judgment. INEC says it will review the certified judgment and take legal advice. Separately, Seyi Makinde has confirmed consultations with Atiku and Peter Obi, but no common ticket or programme has been announced. The NDC says it wants support for Obi and Kwankwaso. Existing party nominations and the statutory timetable mean an endorsement does not automatically replace candidates on INEC's list. The NDC has challenged the Tinubu administration over capital-budget releases, citing a health allocation figure previously disclosed by the health minister. The APC rejects the criticism. The NDC's wider claims about political donations require separate documentary evidence. Nigeria's annual headline inflation eased to 14.06% in October, but month-on-month headline prices rose 0.43%; annual food inflation remained 19.13%.

AFRICA — Mozambique opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane has gone on trial on charges including instigating terrorism and inciting civil disobedience after he rejected the disputed 2024 election. He denies wrongdoing and says he advocated electoral transparency; the Supreme Court president denies political influence. Sudan and Ethiopia are accusing each other of supporting armed groups. Both governments deny the allegations, which AP says it could not independently verify. The DRC Ebola outbreak remains serious: the ECDC's 16 November update recorded 11,376 confirmed cases and 5,568 related deaths using data through 14 November. Nigeria says its single reported case was discharged and all 62 identified contacts completed monitoring. The Gambia's electoral commission has cleared President Adama Barrow and eight other candidates for December's presidential election; clearance is not an election result.

UNITED STATES, CANADA AND BUSINESS — US export controls on advanced AI chips and remote data-centre access are increasing compliance pressure on companies operating in Asia and Brazil. Canada and China have agreed to remove selected tariffs on Canadian pork and seafood exports worth about C$400 million annually, while Canada extends tariff-remission measures for selected Chinese steel and aluminium products. Oil prices eased in early trading as supply-surplus expectations outweighed immediate Gulf security concerns, although the Hormuz shipping risk remains. The EBRD warns that developing economies could miss AI productivity gains without reliable electricity, compute, finance, skills and industrial capacity.

PUBLIC INTEREST AND EDITORIAL STANDARD — RadiantWaves distinguishes verified events from official claims, allegations, political proposals and legal applications. An appeal is not a stay; a campaign pledge is not enacted policy; a planned summit is not an agreement; and a reported casualty figure remains attributed where it cannot be independently verified. featured.title: Gombe's conditional reconciliation offer leaves ADC leadership and Atiku nomination unresolved
featured.summary: Nafiu Bala Gombe says he is willing to work with Atiku Abubakar and David Mark if party membership and constitutional rules are respected. The Mark-led faction has appealed and sought a stay, but no stay order or reconciliation agreement was verified.
featured.content: Nafiu Bala Gombe, whose lawsuit produced the 5 November Federal High Court judgment affecting the David Mark-led ADC leadership, has offered conditional reconciliation to Atiku Abubakar, David Mark and other party figures. In an interview with BBC Hausa, reported by Nigerian media, Gombe said the judgment should not be used to victimise opponents. He insists that those seeking leadership or elective office must meet the ADC constitution's requirements, including ward-level registration and payment of membership dues. Rauf Aregbesola, national secretary in the Mark-led faction, has appealed and applied for a stay of execution, arguing that the court lacked jurisdiction and relying on an earlier ruling. INEC says it will examine the certified judgment and take legal advice. An appeal and an application for a stay do not by themselves suspend a judgment. Premium Times reported that the ADC had not obtained a court order granting a stay as of Monday. Neither faction has announced an agreement on leadership, earlier decisions or Atiku's nomination. The court orders do not expressly name Atiku in the final orders, but the legal consequences for the primaries and nominations remain contested.

topStories.title: Trump meets Quad leaders in Manila as Indo-Pacific security and technology move to the centre of diplomacy
topStories.country: Philippines / United States / India / Japan / Australia
topStories.summary: Donald Trump has met Narendra Modi, Anthony Albanese and Sanae Takaichi in Manila in the first Quad leaders' meeting since his return to the White House. Public remarks point to maritime security, critical minerals, energy resilience and emerging technologies as priorities; detailed private discussions and any agreed measures remain to be confirmed.
topStories.content: US President Donald Trump met the leaders of India, Australia and Japan in Manila on Tuesday, bringing together the four members of the Quad for their first leaders' meeting since Trump returned to office in January 2025. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said critical minerals, rare earths and artificial intelligence were among the subjects for the closed discussion. Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi emphasised a free and open Indo-Pacific, economic security, energy and emerging technologies. India's Narendra Modi highlighted the group's work on maritime security. Trump announced a maritime-patrol-aircraft exercise, describing it as a way to protect regional peace; that is his stated rationale, not an independent assessment of the exercise's effect. The meeting comes amid tension over the South China Sea, Taiwan, US-China technology controls and the US-led Pax Silica initiative. Demonstrations in Manila have included criticism of the initiative's planned technology hub, with opponents raising concerns about local energy and water resources and the rights of Indigenous communities. No joint statement or detailed policy agreement should be assumed until the governments publish their readouts.

topStories.title: Kyiv reports damage to critical infrastructure after overnight Russian strikes
topStories.summary: Ukrainian officials report damage to Kyiv's underground railway and critical infrastructure after overnight attacks. Russia says it launched a large strike against military-industrial sites, energy facilities and other targets; those claims are attributed to the Russian Defence Ministry.
topStories.content: Kyiv experienced heavy overnight attacks, with city officials reporting damage to the metro system and critical infrastructure. Ukraine's capital administration urged residents to seek shelter after explosions. Russia's Defence Ministry said its forces launched a large strike using missiles and drones against military-industrial sites in Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia, Cherkasy and Dnipropetrovsk, and claimed to have hit energy facilities, port infrastructure and vessels used by Ukraine's armed forces. Those descriptions are the Russian military's account; they should not be treated as independently verified assessments of every target. Separately, Moscow's mayor said hundreds of drones had been directed towards the Russian capital, while Russia's Defence Ministry claimed large numbers were intercepted. Ukrainian and Russian claims about the scale and results of drone operations require independent verification. The attacks underline the continued vulnerability of urban infrastructure and energy systems as winter approaches.

topStories.title: France's public-sector strike disrupts transport as unions demand immediate pay rises
topStories.summary: Public-sector unions are mobilising across France over salaries and purchasing power. Le Monde reports transport disruption in several regions, some ports affected and Paris metro stations closed for demonstrations; the TGV network was not reported disrupted in the update reviewed.
topStories.content: France is experiencing a nationwide day of public-sector mobilisation after unions rejected government proposals on pay. The CGT, FO, CFDT, UNSA, FSU, Solidaires, CFE-CGC and FAFP are among the organisations calling for immediate increases. The unions say the public-sector salary index has been frozen for a fourth year and argue that some basic public-service pay scales will remain below the private-sector minimum wage after the next minimum-wage adjustment. The government, led by Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, has proposed a month of discussions on several issues, including urgent measures for the lowest-paid workers, and plans to meet unions again on 11 December. Unions say this does not replace general salary increases. Le Monde's live coverage reported train disruption in several regions, some ports affected and several Paris metro stations closed for demonstrations. The TGV network was not reported disrupted in the update reviewed. The strike comes amid wider cost-of-living protests and pressure on the 2027 budget.

topStories.title: Germany urges Israel to expand humanitarian access to Gaza before winter
topStories.summary: German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul says significantly more humanitarian aid must reach Gaza before the winter rains. Germany says new cargo scanners are expected to increase the flow of goods, while the EU continues to call for sustained access and protection of civilians.
topStories.content: Germany's Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has urged Israel to allow substantially more humanitarian assistance into Gaza as rainy and stormy winter weather approaches. He said Germany had supplied cargo scanners for trucks and welcomed an Israeli security-cabinet decision to begin using them, while warning that the humanitarian situation remains severe. The European Union's 14 November statement also called for immediate, unimpeded and sustained aid access, the reopening of all Gaza crossings and protection for civilians, medical personnel and infrastructure. The EU said flooding and winter conditions were worsening living conditions for an already exhausted population. The EU also called for implementation of the wider ceasefire framework and reiterated its support for a two-state solution. These are diplomatic demands; they do not establish that aid access has improved sufficiently or that all parties are complying with their obligations. Humanitarian agencies continue to assess the needs on the ground.

topStories.title: Canada and China expand trade concessions after Carney-Xi meeting in Shenzhen
topStories.summary: Mark Carney and Xi Jinping have agreed to expand tariff concessions covering Canadian pork and seafood exports and selected Chinese steel and aluminium products. Ottawa says the Canadian exports covered represent about C$400 million annually.
topStories.content: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Tuesday as both governments seek more predictable commercial relations. Canada's trade office says China will remove a 25% tariff on selected Canadian frozen pork cuts and seafood products, including cold-water shrimp, Greenland halibut, certain molluscs and sea cucumber. Ottawa says the exports involved are worth approximately C$400 million a year. Canada, in turn, is extending and broadening tariff-remission measures for selected Chinese steel and aluminium products where domestic supply is insufficient or unavailable. Carney described the arrangement as a step towards greater predictability and stability. The agreement is a targeted trade adjustment, not a comprehensive free-trade deal. It also unfolds against a difficult backdrop: Canada remains concerned about Chinese state-linked competition and security issues, while seeking to reduce reliance on the US market.

topStories.title: Mozambique opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane goes on trial over post-election protests
topStories.summary: Opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane has appeared before Mozambique's Supreme Court on charges including instigating terrorism and inciting civil disobedience. He denies wrongdoing and says he advocated electoral transparency; the court's president denies political influence.
topStories.content: Mozambique's opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane went on trial on Tuesday over his role in protests that followed the disputed 2024 election. Prosecutors accuse him of offences including instigating terrorism and inciting civil disobedience; he denies the charges and says he was advocating electoral transparency after rejecting the result. The election kept the long-ruling Frelimo party in power and was questioned by observers who reported irregularities in vote counting and the alteration of some results. Months of protests followed. Amnesty International, citing local civic groups, said more than 300 people were killed during the unrest, while Human Rights Watch alleged security forces used live ammunition. Those casualty and responsibility claims are attributed to the organisations and have not been independently adjudicated in Mondlane's trial. His party describes the prosecution as political; the Supreme Court president denies political influence and says the case will be decided according to law. If convicted of the most serious charge, Mondlane could face up to 24 years in prison.

topStories.title: Marine Le Pen's pension plan faces questions over savings and France's public finances
topStories.summary: Marine Le Pen is presenting National Rally pension proposals as the party faces investor scrutiny. The party says its plan could save €15–20 billion annually, but economists and investors question how that fits with reversing Macron's retirement reform.
topStories.content: Marine Le Pen is due to set out pension proposals as the National Rally seeks to reconcile a popular pledge to allow some early starters to retire at 60 with promises to restore France's public finances. Pensions are the country's largest area of public spending and are expected to exceed €430 billion next year. Le Pen has promised €140 billion in overall budget savings by 2032 and says pension changes could eventually save €15–20 billion annually. Investors and economists question whether those targets can be achieved while reversing the 2023 reform that raised the statutory retirement age to 64. Recent National Rally comments place greater emphasis on years of contributions: some workers could retire between 60 and 62 after 40–42 years of contributions, depending on when they started work. Many graduates would still need to work into their 60s to receive full benefits. The party has also proposed tightening contribution rules, encouraging employers to retain older workers and creating a sovereign-wealth-style fund. These are opposition proposals, not enacted policy or independently verified savings.

topStories.background: The National Rally is seeking to broaden its economic credibility ahead of the 2027 presidential election, while French bond markets are sensitive to the country's deficit and debt trajectory.
topStories.whyItMatters: The proposals may influence the election debate on retirement, intergenerational fairness and fiscal sustainability. Their credibility depends on detailed costing and clear rules about contribution years.
topStories.whatHappensNext: Watch the full policy presentation, independent fiscal analysis, reactions from unions and rival parties, and whether the party publishes a complete financing plan.

topStories.title: Atiku, Makinde and Obi consultations expose the legal and political limits of an opposition alliance
topStories.summary: Seyi Makinde has confirmed consultations with Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi on presidential cooperation, but no common ticket or joint programme has been announced. Existing party nominations and statutory withdrawal and merger deadlines constrain what any agreement can change.
topStories.content: Opposition leaders are discussing cooperation ahead of Nigeria's 16 January presidential election, but the talks remain politically and legally complicated. Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde has confirmed consultations with former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi, while declining to endorse a preferred candidate or identify a settled method for choosing one. The NDC has separately said it wants other opposition figures to support its Obi-Kwankwaso ticket. The party's spokesperson could not confirm a formal proposal or NDC participation in the Atiku-Makinde discussions. Premium Times reports that Atiku and Rotimi Amaechi are listed for the ADC, Obi and Rabiu Kwankwaso for the NDC, and Makinde and Lawal Daura for the APM. Under the ordinary timetable described in the 2026 Electoral Act, the deadline for a candidate's signed withdrawal to reach INEC was 18 October; formal party mergers require a separate process and notice. A political endorsement may influence supporters, but it does not automatically replace a candidate on INEC's list. No common ticket or joint policy programme has been announced.

topStories.summary: Beijing says it will take necessary measures after new US rules restrict remote access to advanced AI chips and servers through data centres in several third countries. The dispute adds pressure to the technology relationship ahead of the Trump-Xi meeting expected in Shenzhen.
topStories.content: China's Foreign Ministry has criticised new US export-control rules that restrict remote access to advanced AI chips and servers through data centres in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil. Spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Beijing would take measures to protect its interests and accused Washington of stretching national-security arguments to suppress Chinese technology development. The US Commerce Department says the rules close a route through which Chinese companies could access restricted computing power using overseas facilities. The measures are not a blanket prohibition on all data-centre activity in those countries; their effect depends on the users, equipment, transactions and licensing requirements. The timing is sensitive because Trump is due to meet Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Thursday. The dispute also creates compliance questions for cloud providers, chip distributors and governments seeking to attract data-centre investment.

topStories.title: Nigeria's annual inflation eases to 14.06%, but monthly headline prices rise
topStories.summary: Annual headline inflation fell to 14.06% in October from 14.63% in September, while annual food inflation stood at 19.13%. The NBS recorded a 0.43% month-on-month rise in headline inflation, so lower annual inflation does not mean the general price level fell.
topStories.content: Nigeria's annual headline inflation rate eased to 14.06% in October from 14.63% in September, according to National Bureau of Statistics data reported by Reuters. Food inflation fell to 19.13% year-on-year from 19.59%. The monthly picture is more mixed: headline inflation rose 0.43% month-on-month, compared with 0.06% in September, while the food sub-index fell 0.75% month-on-month. The food decline was smaller than the 1.55% fall recorded in September. Core inflation stood at 10.78% year-on-year and contracted 0.53% month-on-month. These figures show a slower annual rate of price increases and some monthly relief in food, but they do not mean that the overall price level has returned to where it was before the cost-of-living shock. Household experience also varies by location, income and spending pattern. The government will need to show that the moderation is sustained and translates into more affordable food, transport, energy and stronger real wages.

topStories.background: Annual inflation measures the change in prices over 12 months. Month-on-month inflation measures the change between the latest two months. They can move in different directions.
topStories.whyItMatters: Lower annual inflation may signal slower price increases, but households can still face high prices and a renewed monthly rise. Food remains particularly important because it takes a large share of household spending.
topStories.whatHappensNext: Watch the next NBS CPI release, food prices, exchange-rate stability, transport costs, real wages and whether household purchasing power improves.

topStories.title: Sudan and Ethiopia trade accusations of backing armed groups as regional tensions rise
topStories.summary: Sudan says Ethiopia is allowing the Rapid Support Forces to operate from its territory; Ethiopia accuses Sudan of supporting Tigrayan rebels. Both governments deny the allegations and AP says it could not independently verify them.
topStories.content: Tensions between Sudan and Ethiopia have increased as the two governments accuse each other of supporting armed groups fighting inside their borders. Sudan's military says Ethiopia has allowed the Rapid Support Forces, which are fighting the Sudanese army, to establish camps, launch drones and stage cross-border attacks. worldNews.content: Mozambique's opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane went on trial on Tuesday over his role in protests that followed the disputed 2024 election. Amnesty International, citing local civic groups, said more than 300 people were killed during the unrest, while Human Rights Watch alleged security forces used live ammunition. Those casualty and responsibility claims are attributed to the organisations and have not been independently adjudicated in Mondlane's trial. His party describes the prosecution as political; the Supreme Court president denies political influence and says the case will be decided according to law. If convicted of the most serious charge, Mondlane could face up to 24 years in prison.

worldNews.country: Democratic Republic of the Congo / Nigeria
worldNews.summary: The ECDC's 16 November update recorded 11,376 confirmed Ebola cases and 5,568 related deaths in the DRC using data through 14 November. Nigeria says its single reported case was discharged and all 62 identified contacts completed monitoring.
worldNews.content: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo remains a major public-health emergency. Nigeria's completed contact monitoring is reassuring but does not remove the need for surveillance, infection prevention, laboratory readiness and transparent public communication. The ECDC has assessed the risk to the general population in the European Union as low. Local health systems in affected areas still need sustained resources and access to treatment and protective equipment.

The timing is sensitive because Trump is due to meet Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Thursday. The dispute also creates compliance questions for cloud providers, chip distributors and governments seeking to attract data-centre investment.

articles.title: Trump meets Quad leaders in Manila as Indo-Pacific security and technology move to the centre of diplomacy
articles.country: Philippines / United States / India / Japan / Australia
articles.summary: Donald Trump has met Narendra Modi, Anthony Albanese and Sanae Takaichi in Manila in the first Quad leaders' meeting since his return to the White House. Public remarks point to maritime security, critical minerals, energy resilience and emerging technologies as priorities; detailed private discussions and any agreed measures remain to be confirmed.
articles.content: US President Donald Trump met the leaders of India, Australia and Japan in Manila on Tuesday, bringing together the four members of the Quad for their first leaders' meeting since Trump returned to office in January 2025. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said critical minerals, rare earths and artificial intelligence were among the subjects for the closed discussion. Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi emphasised a free and open Indo-Pacific, economic security, energy and emerging technologies. India's Narendra Modi highlighted the group's work on maritime security. Trump announced a maritime-patrol-aircraft exercise, describing it as a way to protect regional peace; that is his stated rationale, not an independent assessment of the exercise's effect. The meeting comes amid tension over the South China Sea, Taiwan, US-China technology controls and the US-led Pax Silica initiative. Demonstrations in Manila have included criticism of the initiative's planned technology hub, with opponents raising concerns about local energy and water resources and the rights of Indigenous communities. No joint statement or detailed policy agreement should be assumed until the governments publish their readouts.

articles.imageNote: Photograph of the Quad leaders at their Manila meeting; Mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty Images via The Guardian.
articles.source: The Guardian live coverage; official leaders' remarks

Reuters — Trump to kick off Asia trip with Quad talks in Manila

articles.background: The Quad is a diplomatic grouping of the United States, Japan, India and Australia. Its members cooperate on regional security, infrastructure, technology and maritime issues, while China views the grouping with suspicion.
articles.whyItMatters: The meeting may shape coordination on sea-lane security, supply chains and advanced technology at a time when regional states are balancing economic ties with China against security partnerships with Washington.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for the official Quad statement, details of the maritime exercise, the proposed US-Thailand trade arrangement and whether the leaders announce concrete commitments on critical minerals or AI.

articles.title: China warns of countermeasures after Washington tightens remote access to advanced AI chips
articles.country: China / United States / Singapore / Malaysia / Thailand / Indonesia / Brazil
articles.summary: Beijing says it will take necessary measures after new US rules restrict remote access to advanced AI chips and servers through data centres in several third countries. The dispute adds pressure to the technology relationship ahead of the Trump-Xi meeting expected in Shenzhen.
articles.content: China's Foreign Ministry has criticised new US export-control rules that restrict remote access to advanced AI chips and servers through data centres in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil. Spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Beijing would take measures to protect its interests and accused Washington of stretching national-security arguments to suppress Chinese technology development. The US Commerce Department says the rules close a route through which Chinese companies could access restricted computing power using overseas facilities. The measures are not a blanket prohibition on all data-centre activity in those countries; their effect depends on the users, equipment, transactions and licensing requirements. The timing is sensitive because Trump is due to meet Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Thursday. The dispute also creates compliance questions for cloud providers, chip distributors and governments seeking to attract data-centre investment.

articles.imageNote: Repository AI illustration; not a photograph of a specific data centre or affected company.
articles.source: The Guardian; Reuters; US Commerce Department

sources.name: The Guardian — China pledges necessary measures over US AI chip curbs, 17 November 2026
Reuters — US curbs China's access to AI chips as Trump heads to Asia

articles.background: US restrictions on advanced semiconductors are intended to limit access to technology with commercial and military applications. Companies have sought alternative access through overseas cloud infrastructure.
articles.whyItMatters: Export controls can redirect investment, increase compliance costs and widen the technology divide. Countries hosting data centres face pressure to demonstrate that their facilities are not being used to bypass restrictions.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for the final licensing guidance, China's response, enforcement actions and whether the issue is raised in the Trump-Xi talks.

articles.title: Canada and China expand trade concessions after Carney-Xi meeting in Shenzhen
articles.summary: Mark Carney and Xi Jinping have agreed to expand tariff concessions covering Canadian pork and seafood exports and selected Chinese steel and aluminium products. Ottawa says the Canadian exports covered represent about C$400 million annually.
articles.content: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Tuesday as both governments seek more predictable commercial relations. Canada's trade office says China will remove a 25% tariff on selected Canadian frozen pork cuts and seafood products, including cold-water shrimp, Greenland halibut, certain molluscs and sea cucumber. Ottawa says the exports involved are worth approximately C$400 million a year. Canada, in turn, is extending and broadening tariff-remission measures for selected Chinese steel and aluminium products where domestic supply is insufficient or unavailable. Carney described the arrangement as a step towards greater predictability and stability. The agreement is a targeted trade adjustment, not a comprehensive free-trade deal. It also unfolds against a difficult backdrop: Canada remains concerned about Chinese state-linked competition and security issues, while seeking to reduce reliance on the US market.

articles.title: China confirms planned Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral meeting in Shenzhen on 19 November
articles.summary: Beijing says Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin are expected to discuss world peace during a planned meeting in Shenzhen on 19 November. The meeting has not yet taken place and no agreement or joint outcome has been announced.
articles.content: China has confirmed that a trilateral meeting involving President Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin is planned during Putin's 18–19 November visit to Shenzhen. Chinese officials have described the proposed discussion as focused on world peace, while Kremlin officials say the meeting will be a centrepiece of the visit. The leaders arrive with sharply different priorities: Washington and Beijing are managing a fragile trade and technology relationship; Moscow is seeking relief from diplomatic isolation and support for its position on Ukraine; and all three governments have strategic interests in nuclear stability. It remains unclear how far the agenda will extend beyond the public framing. China has been cautious about joining nuclear-disarmament negotiations because its arsenal is smaller than those of the US and Russia. The meeting is a planned diplomatic event, not evidence of a negotiated settlement on Ukraine, Iran or arms control.

articles.title: France and Malaysia upgrade ties in rare-earths and strategic-industry agreements
articles.summary: Emmanuel Macron and Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced a strategic partnership and cooperation deals, including Malaysia's agreement to relax some raw rare-earth export restrictions for joint processing work with France.
articles.content: France and Malaysia have upgraded their bilateral relationship to a strategic partnership during President Emmanuel Macron's visit to Kuala Lumpur. The two governments announced agreements covering defence, security and industrial cooperation. Malaysia has agreed to relax export restrictions on some raw rare-earth materials to support joint development and processing with France. Macron said the renewed partnership should strengthen the two countries' independence, while Anwar Ibrahim presented the arrangements as an opportunity to build local value and cooperation. Rare earths are essential to electric vehicles, wind turbines, electronics and defence systems, and governments are seeking supply chains less dependent on a small number of producers. The announcement does not mean Malaysia has removed all export controls or that a complete processing industry is already operating. The details of the agreements and implementation will matter.

articles.title: Kyiv reports damage to critical infrastructure after overnight Russian strikes
articles.summary: Ukrainian officials report damage to Kyiv's underground railway and critical infrastructure after overnight attacks. Russia says it launched a large strike against military-industrial sites, energy facilities and other targets; those claims are attributed to the Russian Defence Ministry.
articles.content: Kyiv experienced heavy overnight attacks, with city officials reporting damage to the metro system and critical infrastructure. Ukraine's capital administration urged residents to seek shelter after explosions. Russia's Defence Ministry said its forces launched a large strike using missiles and drones against military-industrial sites in Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia, Cherkasy and Dnipropetrovsk, and claimed to have hit energy facilities, port infrastructure and vessels used by Ukraine's armed forces. Those descriptions are the Russian military's account; they should not be treated as independently verified assessments of every target. Separately, Moscow's mayor said hundreds of drones had been directed towards the Russian capital, while Russia's Defence Ministry claimed large numbers were intercepted. Ukrainian and Russian claims about the scale and results of drone operations require independent verification. The attacks underline the continued vulnerability of urban infrastructure and energy systems as winter approaches.

articles.title: France's public-sector strike disrupts transport as unions demand immediate pay rises
articles.summary: Public-sector unions are mobilising across France over salaries and purchasing power. Le Monde reports transport disruption in several regions, some ports affected and Paris metro stations closed for demonstrations; the TGV network was not reported disrupted in the update reviewed.
articles.content: France is experiencing a nationwide day of public-sector mobilisation after unions rejected government proposals on pay. The CGT, FO, CFDT, UNSA, FSU, Solidaires, CFE-CGC and FAFP are among the organisations calling for immediate increases. The unions say the public-sector salary index has been frozen for a fourth year and argue that some basic public-service pay scales will remain below the private-sector minimum wage after the next minimum-wage adjustment. The government, led by Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, has proposed a month of discussions on several issues, including urgent measures for the lowest-paid workers, and plans to meet unions again on 11 December. Unions say this does not replace general salary increases. Le Monde's live coverage reported train disruption in several regions, some ports affected and several Paris metro stations closed for demonstrations. The TGV network was not reported disrupted in the update reviewed. The strike comes amid wider cost-of-living protests and pressure on the 2027 budget.

articles.title: Marine Le Pen's pension plan faces questions over savings and France's public finances
articles.summary: Marine Le Pen is presenting National Rally pension proposals as the party faces investor scrutiny. The party says its plan could save €15–20 billion annually, but economists and investors question how that fits with reversing Macron's retirement reform.
articles.content: Marine Le Pen is due to set out pension proposals as the National Rally seeks to reconcile a popular pledge to allow some early starters to retire at 60 with promises to restore France's public finances. Pensions are the country's largest area of public spending and are expected to exceed €430 billion next year. Le Pen has promised €140 billion in overall budget savings by 2032 and says pension changes could eventually save €15–20 billion annually. Investors and economists question whether those targets can be achieved while reversing the 2023 reform that raised the statutory retirement age to 64. Recent National Rally comments place greater emphasis on years of contributions: some workers could retire between 60 and 62 after 40–42 years of contributions, depending on when they started work. Many graduates would still need to work into their 60s to receive full benefits. The party has also proposed tightening contribution rules, encouraging employers to retain older workers and creating a sovereign-wealth-style fund. These are opposition proposals, not enacted policy or independently verified savings.

articles.whatHappensNext: Watch the full policy presentation, independent fiscal analysis, reactions from unions and rival parties, and whether the party publishes a complete financing plan.

articles.title: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham says Brexit weakened Britain's global standing and calls for long-term EU debate
articles.summary: Andy Burnham says the UK's position in the world has diminished since Brexit and wants discussions with the EU on the country's long-term relationship. He says the British public must decide the outcome; no immediate return to the EU has been announced.
articles.content: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has used a major foreign-policy speech to argue that Brexit diminished Britain's global standing and that the current UK-EU relationship is not good enough. He says the government will begin discussions with European partners after a Brussels summit scheduled for Friday, exploring options for the long-term relationship, including a customs union, the single market or potentially rejoining the bloc. Burnham has also said the process will take time and that the British public must decide at every stage. Labour's current manifesto commitments still constrain what the government will do before the next general election, and ministers are divided over how quickly to reopen the issue. Burnham says the Friday summit should seek practical agreements on food and farming, emissions trading and youth mobility, which he estimates could raise GDP by 0.4%, or about £17 billion. Conservative opponents argue the focus risks reopening divisions over the 2016 referendum. The speech signals a debate, not a negotiated EU deal or a decision to rejoin.

articles.title: Germany urges Israel to expand humanitarian access to Gaza before winter
articles.summary: German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul says significantly more humanitarian aid must reach Gaza before the winter rains. Germany says new cargo scanners are expected to increase the flow of goods, while the EU continues to call for sustained access and protection of civilians.
articles.content: Germany's Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has urged Israel to allow substantially more humanitarian assistance into Gaza as rainy and stormy winter weather approaches. He said Germany had supplied cargo scanners for trucks and welcomed an Israeli security-cabinet decision to begin using them, while warning that the humanitarian situation remains severe. The European Union's 14 November statement also called for immediate, unimpeded and sustained aid access, the reopening of all Gaza crossings and protection for civilians, medical personnel and infrastructure. The EU said flooding and winter conditions were worsening living conditions for an already exhausted population. The EU also called for implementation of the wider ceasefire framework and reiterated its support for a two-state solution. These are diplomatic demands; they do not establish that aid access has improved sufficiently or that all parties are complying with their obligations. Humanitarian agencies continue to assess the needs on the ground.

articles.title: UK maritime monitor records projectile strike near Strait of Hormuz; responsibility remains unknown
articles.summary: UKMTO recorded an unidentified projectile striking a merchant vessel near the Strait of Hormuz and causing an engine-room fire. All crew were accounted for and no casualties were reported; the attacker and weapon have not been identified.
articles.content: The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported that an unidentified projectile struck a merchant vessel near the Strait of Hormuz in Warning 207-26. The incident caused an engine-room fire. All crew were accounted for and no casualties were reported, but the vessel's identity, extent of damage and any environmental impact were not fully established in the initial warning. UKMTO did not identify the attacker or confirm the weapon used. Separately, Omani and Iranian officials have discussed safeguarding maritime corridors and maintaining the flow of global shipping. Those discussions do not amount to a confirmed agreement restoring normal commercial passage. The strait is a critical route for oil and liquefied natural gas, so even an unattributed incident can affect insurance, freight rates and shipping decisions. RadiantWaves does not attribute responsibility without corroborating evidence.

articles.title: Mozambique opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane goes on trial over post-election protests
articles.summary: Opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane has appeared before Mozambique's Supreme Court on charges including instigating terrorism and inciting civil disobedience. He denies wrongdoing and says he advocated electoral transparency; the court's president denies political influence.
articles.content: Mozambique's opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane went on trial on Tuesday over his role in protests that followed the disputed 2024 election. Prosecutors accuse him of offences including instigating terrorism and inciting civil disobedience; he denies the charges and says he was advocating electoral transparency after rejecting the result. The election kept the long-ruling Frelimo party in power and was questioned by observers who reported irregularities in vote counting and the alteration of some results. Months of protests followed. Amnesty International, citing local civic groups, said more than 300 people were killed during the unrest, while Human Rights Watch alleged security forces used live ammunition. Those casualty and responsibility claims are attributed to the organisations and have not been independently adjudicated in Mondlane's trial. His party describes the prosecution as political; the Supreme Court president denies political influence and says the case will be decided according to law. If convicted of the most serious charge, Mondlane could face up to 24 years in prison.

articles.title: Sudan and Ethiopia trade accusations of backing armed groups as regional tensions rise
articles.summary: Sudan says Ethiopia is allowing the Rapid Support Forces to operate from its territory; Ethiopia accuses Sudan of supporting Tigrayan rebels. Both governments deny the allegations and AP says it could not independently verify them.
articles.content: Tensions between Sudan and Ethiopia have increased as the two governments accuse each other of supporting armed groups fighting inside their borders. Sudan's military says Ethiopia has allowed the Rapid Support Forces, which are fighting the Sudanese army, to establish camps, launch drones and stage cross-border attacks. Sudan has taken complaints to the United Nations and African Union. Ethiopia says Sudan supports rebels in its Tigray region, where fighting resumed in September and broke the 2022 peace agreement. Both countries deny the other's accusations, and the Associated Press says it could not independently verify the claims. The dispute is compounded by regional alliances, the contested Al-Fashaga border and disagreements over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. Sudan's war has killed at least 59,000 people according to ACLED and displaced about 13 million, while renewed fighting in Tigray raises the risk of a wider proxy conflict. Analysts warn that weapons and fighters crossing the border could worsen both crises.

articles.title: DRC Ebola outbreak remains serious as Nigeria completes monitoring of identified contacts
articles.country: Democratic Republic of the Congo / Nigeria
articles.summary: The ECDC's 16 November update recorded 11,376 confirmed Ebola cases and 5,568 related deaths in the DRC using data through 14 November. Nigeria says its single reported case was discharged and all 62 identified contacts completed monitoring.
articles.content: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo remains a major public-health emergency. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control's 16 November update recorded 11,376 confirmed cases and 5,568 related deaths, using data through 14 November. Nigeria's response has a different status: the one reported patient was discharged on 11 November and all 62 identified contacts completed monitoring. These figures refer to different national situations and reporting periods and should not be conflated. Nigeria's completed contact monitoring is reassuring but does not remove the need for surveillance, infection prevention, laboratory readiness and transparent public communication. The ECDC has assessed the risk to the general population in the European Union as low. Local health systems in affected areas still need sustained resources and access to treatment and protective equipment.

articles.title: Gombe's conditional reconciliation offer leaves ADC leadership and Atiku nomination unresolved
articles.summary: Nafiu Bala Gombe says he is willing to work with Atiku Abubakar and David Mark if party membership and constitutional rules are respected. The Mark-led faction has appealed and sought a stay, but no stay order or reconciliation agreement was verified.
articles.content: Nafiu Bala Gombe, whose lawsuit produced the 5 November Federal High Court judgment affecting the David Mark-led ADC leadership, has offered conditional reconciliation to Atiku Abubakar, David Mark and other party figures. In an interview with BBC Hausa, reported by Nigerian media, Gombe said the judgment should not be used to victimise opponents. He insists that those seeking leadership or elective office must meet the ADC constitution's requirements, including ward-level registration and payment of membership dues. Rauf Aregbesola, national secretary in the Mark-led faction, has appealed and applied for a stay of execution, arguing that the court lacked jurisdiction and relying on an earlier ruling. INEC says it will examine the certified judgment and take legal advice. An appeal and an application for a stay do not by themselves suspend a judgment. Premium Times reported that the ADC had not obtained a court order granting a stay as of Monday. Neither faction has announced an agreement on leadership, earlier decisions or Atiku's nomination. The court orders do not expressly name Atiku in the final orders, but the legal consequences for the primaries and nominations remain contested.

articles.title: Atiku, Makinde and Obi consultations expose the legal and political limits of an opposition alliance
articles.summary: Seyi Makinde has confirmed consultations with Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi on presidential cooperation, but no common ticket or joint programme has been announced. Existing party nominations and statutory withdrawal and merger deadlines constrain what any agreement can change.
articles.content: Opposition leaders are discussing cooperation ahead of Nigeria's 16 January presidential election, but the talks remain politically and legally complicated. Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde has confirmed consultations with former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi, while declining to endorse a preferred candidate or identify a settled method for choosing one. The NDC has separately said it wants other opposition figures to support its Obi-Kwankwaso ticket. The party's spokesperson could not confirm a formal proposal or NDC participation in the Atiku-Makinde discussions. Premium Times reports that Atiku and Rotimi Amaechi are listed for the ADC, Obi and Rabiu Kwankwaso for the NDC, and Makinde and Lawal Daura for the APM. Under the ordinary timetable described in the 2026 Electoral Act, the deadline for a candidate's signed withdrawal to reach INEC was 18 October; formal party mergers require a separate process and notice. A political endorsement may influence supporters, but it does not automatically replace a candidate on INEC's list. No common ticket or joint policy programme has been announced.

articles.title: NDC challenges Tinubu administration over health spending as APC rejects opposition criticism
articles.summary: The NDC cites a reported ₦36 million release from a ₦218 billion 2025 health capital allocation, a figure previously disclosed by the health minister to lawmakers. The APC dismisses the party's criticism; the NDC has not produced evidence linking government funds to pro-Tinubu campaign gifts.
articles.content: The Nigeria Democratic Congress has challenged the Tinubu administration over capital-budget releases for health and defence and questioned the apparent availability of resources for political publicity and gifts distributed by groups supporting the president. Its criticism centred on a figure of ₦36 million released from a ₦218 billion 2025 capital allocation to the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare. Premium Times traced that figure to Health Minister Mohammed Pate's disclosure to lawmakers in February, when he said capital spending was constrained by inadequate cash releases even though personnel costs had been fully released. The NDC also alleged that only about 7% of the defence capital budget was released, but Premium Times said that figure had not been confirmed against official budget records. The party has not produced records showing that publicity campaigns or donated items were financed with government funds. The APC's Felix Morka dismissed the criticism as political posturing but did not provide alternative figures for the health and defence releases or identify the sources of the donations. The budget-release issue and the financing of political donations are separate questions and require documentary scrutiny.

articles.title: Nigeria's annual inflation eases to 14.06%, but monthly headline prices rise
articles.summary: Annual headline inflation fell to 14.06% in October from 14.63% in September, while annual food inflation stood at 19.13%. The NBS recorded a 0.43% month-on-month rise in headline inflation, so lower annual inflation does not mean the general price level fell.
articles.content: Nigeria's annual headline inflation rate eased to 14.06% in October from 14.63% in September, according to National Bureau of Statistics data reported by Reuters. Food inflation fell to 19.13% year-on-year from 19.59%. The monthly picture is more mixed: headline inflation rose 0.43% month-on-month, compared with 0.06% in September, while the food sub-index fell 0.75% month-on-month. The food decline was smaller than the 1.55% fall recorded in September. Core inflation stood at 10.78% year-on-year and contracted 0.53% month-on-month. These figures show a slower annual rate of price increases and some monthly relief in food, but they do not mean that the overall price level has returned to where it was before the cost-of-living shock. Household experience also varies by location, income and spending pattern. The government will need to show that the moderation is sustained and translates into more affordable food, transport, energy and stronger real wages.

The decision confirms that the candidates have met the commission's requirements to appear on the ballot; it does not indicate who is likely to win. Barrow is seeking a third term, making the campaign important to ongoing debate about presidential tenure, constitutional rules and democratic competition. The opposition faces the challenge of presenting a credible alternative while scrutinising the administration's record. The election will also test the strength of electoral institutions and public confidence after years of political debate over term limits and governance.

articles.summary: New US rules require additional licensing and end-user controls for certain advanced AI chips and remote computing access through overseas data centres. The measures are aimed at limiting diversion to restricted users, including Chinese firms.
articles.content: The US Commerce Department has tightened controls on advanced artificial-intelligence chips and remote access to computing power through overseas data centres. The rules are designed to close a route through which restricted users could obtain access to advanced chips by using facilities in third countries. The affected countries named in reporting include Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil. The restrictions do not prohibit every chip sale or every data-centre service in those markets; transactions and end users determine whether licensing or additional checks apply. The policy comes as the Trump administration prepares for talks with Xi Jinping and as technology investors reassess the cost of compliance. Companies in Southeast Asia may need stronger customer checks, more detailed end-user records and legal review of cross-border cloud arrangements. China has criticised the move and threatened necessary countermeasures.

articles.title: Oil markets weigh supply-surplus expectations against renewed Gulf shipping risk
articles.summary: Reuters reported Brent at US$91.66 and US WTI at US$84.99 in early trading, with prices easing as expectations of a fourth-quarter supply surplus offset concern about shipping disruption near Hormuz.
articles.content: Oil prices eased in early Tuesday trading as expectations of a fourth-quarter supply surplus outweighed renewed concern about attacks on shipping in the Gulf. Reuters reported Brent crude down 0.8% at US$91.66 a barrel and US West Texas Intermediate down 0.9% at US$84.99. The International Energy Agency expects the market to return to surplus in the fourth quarter as Middle East exports recover faster than demand. That outlook does not mean maritime security risks have passed: the Strait of Hormuz remains a critical route and tanker incidents can quickly affect insurance, freight and delivery decisions. For oil-importing economies, the domestic effect depends on exchange rates, taxes, fuel pricing, transport costs and the extent to which international price movements are passed through to consumers. For producers such as Nigeria, lower benchmark prices can also affect public revenue forecasts.

articles.title: EBRD warns developing economies could miss the AI productivity boom without power, skills and finance
articles.summary: The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development warns that emerging economies need reliable power, skills, finance and industrial capacity to capture AI-related productivity gains. Access to technology alone will not guarantee broad economic benefits.
articles.content: The EBRD's Transition Report 2026–27 warns that developing economies risk missing the productivity and investment opportunities associated with artificial intelligence and defence-related industries if they do not strengthen basic infrastructure and skills. Reliable electricity, affordable computing, broadband, research institutions, access to finance and predictable regulation all affect whether businesses can adopt AI and develop their own products. Countries that lack these foundations may remain consumers of foreign platforms rather than producers of technology, services and intellectual property. The warning is relevant to African economies, including Nigeria, where digital adoption is advancing but energy reliability, skills gaps and financing costs remain obstacles. The report does not suggest that every economy should pursue the same AI strategy; it points to the need for policies suited to local industrial strengths and public needs.

The proposal would allow neighbouring countries to make use of available storage capacity in Japan, potentially improving the region's ability to respond to supply disruptions. Southeast Asian economies generally hold smaller oil stockpiles than Japan and have been exposed to higher prices and tighter supplies as conflict disrupts shipping and trade. The proposal was discussed during the ASEAN summit in Manila. It is not yet a fully implemented regional reserve system; the details would require agreement on access, financing, release triggers and logistics. The initiative is part of a wider effort to strengthen energy resilience while the region navigates geopolitical competition and uncertainty around key sea lanes.

articles.summary: Papua New Guinea's Prime Minister James Marape told Xi Jinping that Taiwan no longer operates in his country and voiced support for China's reunification position. The statement reflects Port Moresby's diplomatic position; it does not resolve the wider Taiwan dispute.
articles.content: Papua New Guinea's Prime Minister James Marape met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen and said Taiwan no longer operates in Papua New Guinea, adding that he hoped this would assist China's efforts towards reunification. The remarks drew attention because Taiwan's status remains one of the most sensitive issues in China's relations with the United States, Japan and other regional governments. Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China and has not ruled out using force to achieve unification. Taiwan operates as a self-governing democracy and rejects Beijing's sovereignty claim. Statements by Pacific governments can affect diplomatic recognition, aid relationships and regional security calculations, but they do not change Taiwan's political status or settle the dispute. europeNews.title: Marine Le Pen's pension plan faces questions over savings and France's public finances
europeNews.summary: Marine Le Pen is presenting National Rally pension proposals as the party faces investor scrutiny. The party says its plan could save €15–20 billion annually, but economists and investors question how that fits with reversing Macron's retirement reform.
europeNews.content: Marine Le Pen is due to set out pension proposals as the National Rally seeks to reconcile a popular pledge to allow some early starters to retire at 60 with promises to restore France's public finances. Pensions are the country's largest area of public spending and are expected to exceed €430 billion next year. Le Pen has promised €140 billion in overall budget savings by 2032 and says pension changes could eventually save €15–20 billion annually. Investors and economists question whether those targets can be achieved while reversing the 2023 reform that raised the statutory retirement age to 64. Recent National Rally comments place greater emphasis on years of contributions: some workers could retire between 60 and 62 after 40–42 years of contributions, depending on when they started work. Many graduates would still need to work into their 60s to receive full benefits. The party has also proposed tightening contribution rules, encouraging employers to retain older workers and creating a sovereign-wealth-style fund. These are opposition proposals, not enacted policy or independently verified savings.

europeNews.title: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham says Brexit weakened Britain's global standing and calls for long-term EU debate
europeNews.summary: Andy Burnham says the UK's position in the world has diminished since Brexit and wants discussions with the EU on the country's long-term relationship. He says the British public must decide the outcome; no immediate return to the EU has been announced.
europeNews.content: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has used a major foreign-policy speech to argue that Brexit diminished Britain's global standing and that the current UK-EU relationship is not good enough. He says the government will begin discussions with European partners after a Brussels summit scheduled for Friday, exploring options for the long-term relationship, including a customs union, the single market or potentially rejoining the bloc. Burnham has also said the process will take time and that the British public must decide at every stage. Labour's current manifesto commitments still constrain what the government will do before the next general election, and ministers are divided over how quickly to reopen the issue. Burnham says the Friday summit should seek practical agreements on food and farming, emissions trading and youth mobility, which he estimates could raise GDP by 0.4%, or about £17 billion. Conservative opponents argue the focus risks reopening divisions over the 2016 referendum. The speech signals a debate, not a negotiated EU deal or a decision to rejoin.

The EU said flooding and winter conditions were worsening living conditions for an already exhausted population. The EU also called for implementation of the wider ceasefire framework and reiterated its support for a two-state solution. These are diplomatic demands; they do not establish that aid access has improved sufficiently or that all parties are complying with their obligations. africaNews.title: Mozambique opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane goes on trial over post-election protests
africaNews.summary: Opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane has appeared before Mozambique's Supreme Court on charges including instigating terrorism and inciting civil disobedience. He denies wrongdoing and says he advocated electoral transparency; the court's president denies political influence.
africaNews.content: Mozambique's opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane went on trial on Tuesday over his role in protests that followed the disputed 2024 election. Prosecutors accuse him of offences including instigating terrorism and inciting civil disobedience; he denies the charges and says he was advocating electoral transparency after rejecting the result. The election kept the long-ruling Frelimo party in power and was questioned by observers who reported irregularities in vote counting and the alteration of some results. Months of protests followed. Amnesty International, citing local civic groups, said more than 300 people were killed during the unrest, while Human Rights Watch alleged security forces used live ammunition. Those casualty and responsibility claims are attributed to the organisations and have not been independently adjudicated in Mondlane's trial. His party describes the prosecution as political; the Supreme Court president denies political influence and says the case will be decided according to law. If convicted of the most serious charge, Mondlane could face up to 24 years in prison.

africaNews.content: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo remains a major public-health emergency. Nigeria's response has a different status: the one reported patient was discharged on 11 November and all 62 identified contacts completed monitoring. These figures refer to different national situations and reporting periods and should not be conflated. Nigeria's completed contact monitoring is reassuring but does not remove the need for surveillance, infection prevention, laboratory readiness and transparent public communication. The ECDC has assessed the risk to the general population in the European Union as low. Local health systems in affected areas still need sustained resources and access to treatment and protective equipment.

Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde has confirmed consultations with former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi, while declining to endorse a preferred candidate or identify a settled method for choosing one. Under the ordinary timetable described in the 2026 Electoral Act, the deadline for a candidate's signed withdrawal to reach INEC was 18 October; formal party mergers require a separate process and notice. The government will need to show that the moderation is sustained and translates into more affordable food, transport, energy and stronger real wages.

asiaNews.title: Trump meets Quad leaders in Manila as Indo-Pacific security and technology move to the centre of diplomacy
asiaNews.country: Philippines / United States / India / Japan / Australia
asiaNews.summary: Donald Trump has met Narendra Modi, Anthony Albanese and Sanae Takaichi in Manila in the first Quad leaders' meeting since his return to the White House. Public remarks point to maritime security, critical minerals, energy resilience and emerging technologies as priorities; detailed private discussions and any agreed measures remain to be confirmed.
asiaNews.content: US President Donald Trump met the leaders of India, Australia and Japan in Manila on Tuesday, bringing together the four members of the Quad for their first leaders' meeting since Trump returned to office in January 2025. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said critical minerals, rare earths and artificial intelligence were among the subjects for the closed discussion. Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi emphasised a free and open Indo-Pacific, economic security, energy and emerging technologies. India's Narendra Modi highlighted the group's work on maritime security. The meeting comes amid tension over the South China Sea, Taiwan, US-China technology controls and the US-led Pax Silica initiative. Demonstrations in Manila have included criticism of the initiative's planned technology hub, with opponents raising concerns about local energy and water resources and the rights of Indigenous communities. asiaNews.title: Canada and China expand trade concessions after Carney-Xi meeting in Shenzhen
asiaNews.summary: Mark Carney and Xi Jinping have agreed to expand tariff concessions covering Canadian pork and seafood exports and selected Chinese steel and aluminium products. Ottawa says the Canadian exports covered represent about C$400 million annually.
asiaNews.content: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Tuesday as both governments seek more predictable commercial relations. Canada's trade office says China will remove a 25% tariff on selected Canadian frozen pork cuts and seafood products, including cold-water shrimp, Greenland halibut, certain molluscs and sea cucumber. Ottawa says the exports involved are worth approximately C$400 million a year. Canada, in turn, is extending and broadening tariff-remission measures for selected Chinese steel and aluminium products where domestic supply is insufficient or unavailable. Carney described the arrangement as a step towards greater predictability and stability. The agreement is a targeted trade adjustment, not a comprehensive free-trade deal. It also unfolds against a difficult backdrop: Canada remains concerned about Chinese state-linked competition and security issues, while seeking to reduce reliance on the US market.

asiaNews.title: Japan proposes regional oil-security task force as Asian economies face supply disruption

asiaNews.content: Japan has proposed a regional task force to coordinate oil stockpiling and the release of supplies during emergencies. The proposal would allow neighbouring countries to make use of available storage capacity in Japan, potentially improving the region's ability to respond to supply disruptions. Southeast Asian economies generally hold smaller oil stockpiles than Japan and have been exposed to higher prices and tighter supplies as conflict disrupts shipping and trade. The proposal was discussed during the ASEAN summit in Manila. It is not yet a fully implemented regional reserve system; the details would require agreement on access, financing, release triggers and logistics. The initiative is part of a wider effort to strengthen energy resilience while the region navigates geopolitical competition and uncertainty around key sea lanes.

asiaNews.title: Papua New Guinea's Taiwan statement draws attention at China-APEC meetings
asiaNews.summary: Papua New Guinea's Prime Minister James Marape told Xi Jinping that Taiwan no longer operates in his country and voiced support for China's reunification position. The statement reflects Port Moresby's diplomatic position; it does not resolve the wider Taiwan dispute.
asiaNews.content: Papua New Guinea's Prime Minister James Marape met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen and said Taiwan no longer operates in Papua New Guinea, adding that he hoped this would assist China's efforts towards reunification. The remarks drew attention because Taiwan's status remains one of the most sensitive issues in China's relations with the United States, Japan and other regional governments. Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China and has not ruled out using force to achieve unification. Taiwan operates as a self-governing democracy and rejects Beijing's sovereignty claim. Statements by Pacific governments can affect diplomatic recognition, aid relationships and regional security calculations, but they do not change Taiwan's political status or settle the dispute. The comments came during the APEC summit period, when regional leaders are balancing trade, infrastructure, security and relations with major powers.

businessNews.title: Oil markets weigh supply-surplus expectations against renewed Gulf shipping risk
businessNews.summary: Reuters reported Brent at US$91.66 and US WTI at US$84.99 in early trading, with prices easing as expectations of a fourth-quarter supply surplus offset concern about shipping disruption near Hormuz.
businessNews.content: Oil prices eased in early Tuesday trading as expectations of a fourth-quarter supply surplus outweighed renewed concern about attacks on shipping in the Gulf. Reuters reported Brent crude down 0.8% at US$91.66 a barrel and US West Texas Intermediate down 0.9% at US$84.99. The International Energy Agency expects the market to return to surplus in the fourth quarter as Middle East exports recover faster than demand. That outlook does not mean maritime security risks have passed: the Strait of Hormuz remains a critical route and tanker incidents can quickly affect insurance, freight and delivery decisions. For oil-importing economies, the domestic effect depends on exchange rates, taxes, fuel pricing, transport costs and the extent to which international price movements are passed through to consumers. businessNews.title: EBRD warns developing economies could miss the AI productivity boom without power, skills and finance

businessNews.content: The EBRD's Transition Report 2026–27 warns that developing economies risk missing the productivity and investment opportunities associated with artificial intelligence and defence-related industries if they do not strengthen basic infrastructure and skills. Reliable electricity, affordable computing, broadband, research institutions, access to finance and predictable regulation all affect whether businesses can adopt AI and develop their own products. Countries that lack these foundations may remain consumers of foreign platforms rather than producers of technology, services and intellectual property. The warning is relevant to African economies, including Nigeria, where digital adoption is advancing but energy reliability, skills gaps and financing costs remain obstacles. The report does not suggest that every economy should pursue the same AI strategy; it points to the need for policies suited to local industrial strengths and public needs.

Companies in Southeast Asia may need stronger customer checks, more detailed end-user records and legal review of cross-border cloud arrangements. technologyNews.title: EBRD warns developing economies could miss the AI productivity boom without power, skills and finance
technologyNews.summary: The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development warns that emerging economies need reliable power, skills, finance and industrial capacity to capture AI-related productivity gains. Access to technology alone will not guarantee broad economic benefits.
technologyNews.content: The EBRD's Transition Report 2026–27 warns that developing economies risk missing the productivity and investment opportunities associated with artificial intelligence and defence-related industries if they do not strengthen basic infrastructure and skills. Reliable electricity, affordable computing, broadband, research institutions, access to finance and predictable regulation all affect whether businesses can adopt AI and develop their own products. Countries that lack these foundations may remain consumers of foreign platforms rather than producers of technology, services and intellectual property. The warning is relevant to African economies, including Nigeria, where digital adoption is advancing but energy reliability, skills gaps and financing costs remain obstacles. The report does not suggest that every economy should pursue the same AI strategy; it points to the need for policies suited to local industrial strengths and public needs.

editorial.title: Opposition unity cannot be built on slogans alone
editorial.summary: ADC reconciliation efforts and wider opposition consultations show that cooperation is possible, but credible unity requires transparent rules, lawful nominations and a common programme.
editorial.content: Nigeria's opposition has a legitimate role in challenging the government and presenting alternatives. That role is weakened when party leadership disputes, unclear membership records and competing nomination claims are left unresolved. Gombe's conditional offer to work with Atiku and David Mark is a political opening, not a settlement. Atiku-Makinde-Obi consultations are also not yet a common ticket or agreed policy platform. Parties must explain who has authority to negotiate, how decisions will be made, how running mates and other candidates will be treated and how members can challenge decisions. INEC must follow certified court documents and the law, not political pressure. The government must protect peaceful political activity, and opposition parties must substantiate allegations of violence or misuse of public resources. A credible alternative is built through transparency, policy and respect for institutions.

analysis.title: The Quad, APEC and the limits of summit diplomacy
analysis.summary: The Manila and Shenzhen meetings show how security, AI and critical minerals are becoming inseparable in Indo-Pacific diplomacy.
analysis.content: The Quad's public agenda includes maritime security, critical minerals, energy and AI. China's response to US chip controls and the planned Trump-Xi-Putin meeting add a second layer of great-power competition. The region is not simply choosing between Washington and Beijing: countries such as Malaysia, Singapore, the Philippines and Canada are trying to preserve trade, investment and diplomatic room while responding to pressure from larger powers. A summit photograph or announcement does not establish a policy outcome. The useful test is whether governments publish commitments, finance them and implement safeguards that protect local communities and smaller economies. The Pax Silica debate in the Philippines illustrates that strategic infrastructure can create local environmental and social concerns even when it is presented as a national-security project.

analysis.title: Nigeria's opposition needs a lawful route from consultations to a credible alternative
analysis.summary: The ADC dispute and wider talks involving Atiku, Makinde and Obi demonstrate the difference between political cooperation and legally effective candidate changes.
analysis.content: Opposition consultations can help voters compare programmes and encourage cooperation, but they cannot bypass party constitutions, the Electoral Act or court orders. Atiku's position in the ADC is affected by a leadership judgment whose consequences are still contested. The Mark-led faction has appealed and sought a stay, but no stay order was verified in the reporting reviewed. Separately, Makinde has confirmed consultations with Atiku and Obi, while the NDC says it prefers the Obi-Kwankwaso ticket. Those discussions have not produced a common ticket or programme. The legal timetable for withdrawals and party mergers matters, as do running mates and candidates for other offices. The public should demand a published coalition framework, a clear decision process and a credible policy platform on jobs, security, public services, debt and the cost of living.
